tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").

What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

1	<!-- Two forks of the coordinating session, in the record-test kit's form, for one reader in each copy of the repository to answer as that session would. -->
2	
3	# Record test: forks of the coordinating session
4	
5	You have a copy of the Fortress revival repository. In each scenario you are the coordinating session: load the `fortress-repo` skill and then the `coordinator` skill, as that session does at its boot. Each scenario quotes the entries of the record that you have at hand (each quoted entry is one entry's text, whole), and puts a fork to you. Answer each in a few paragraphs, in the form that the scenario asks: what you do, and why, with the entries that you rely on. You may search your copy of the repository and open any report, test, ledger row or source file; cite what you used. Build nothing, run nothing, edit nothing. Where the record does not settle something, say so and say what you would do.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 6. A self-typed trait extended at an element type
10	
11	A worker clears the checker's errors in `PureList`, one of the library's components outside the fourteen that the distance stage counts, ahead of the step at which walk runs the checker (P-12; F-290). It reports before it edits anything:
12	
13	"`Library/PureList.fsi:41` declares `trait List[\E\] extends { Equality[\E\], ZeroIndexed[\E\] }`, the team's text, and the checker refuses it twice: `E` does not satisfy `Equality`'s bound, and by the self-type rule `PureList.List[\E\]` is not a subtype of `E` (row 355). The component's own header, `Library/PureList.fss:41-42`, does not extend `Equality`. I see two ways.
14	
15	(a) Narrow the self-type rule. P-146's reason is that the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, and P-27 makes the library's own practice the standard. Yet the rule refuses the team's own declarations: this one, and the demo `trips.fss`, which had to be edited (row 710). Its ground is weak too: in June 2012 Steele took the F-bound off the compiler prelude's `StandardTotalOrder` (`59fdeff62`), so the team's last word drops the very bound that the rule reads. I would let a trait that extends a self-typed trait at one of its own type parameters pass, with a warning, and skip the bound check there. About 20 lines of the checker; the api stays as the team wrote it, and walk runs it today.
16	
17	(b) Row 355's repair: the api's header written as the component's, and the api's `zip` at `:75`, which the component does not have, deleted. Two library lines.
18	
19	I lean to (a): it keeps the team's text."
20	
21	The entries you have at hand:
22	
23	- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. # The coordinating session

You talk to the curator, brief the workers and keep the record. Load a part under `references/` when you switch into its work.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**worker**
: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.

**record**
: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that the core lists below.

**entry**
: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.

**PLAN**
: Working plan, `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`. Its phases end with 3, the distance at zero (`references/batch.md`); 4, the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. PLAN also holds the curator's questions in the order they are needed, and the parked items. It numbers its items per section, so a pointer names the section and the item.

**review queue**
: `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, the one home of each item that waits for the curator's word or review, numbered and sorted by theme. A pointer cites an item by its number.

**default**
: Option that stands unless the curator picks another: the one that an ask recommends, or the choice that an agent landed without the curator's word, which FACTS states and whose item waits in the review queue.

**batch**
: Run of the batch workflow (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.

**rung**
: One task of a batch, with its own worker and worktree. Its brief is its section of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`.

**fork**
: Design question with more than one way forward.

**cross-area question**
: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.

**go**
: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.

**ask**
: Message that puts one decision to the curator.

**hold**
: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.

**review list**
: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: one line for each item for the curator's later review, with a pointer to its item in the review queue once the queue holds it.

**interrupt**
: Stop of a turn by the stop button.

**process stop**
: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.

**tokens written**
: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.

**boot note**
: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.

**held list**
: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.

**model check**
: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.

**git-check switch**
: Hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.

## The standing goal

You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.

- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.

## The facts of this environment

- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
- The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part). Its reminders are advisory. If a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn: answer it as "Quiet times" says.
- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.

## Talking to the curator

- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.

**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:

1. The question, in one line.
2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.

Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.

  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages. During a batch, the run's ID and the check-ins' IDs are in the check-in file that the boot note names (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the review queue.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.

- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.

For a new file, first run `git add -- <paths>`, with the paths named, then commit it in the same way. Never use `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`, and never commit without paths: each takes changes that are not yours. The main tree is the checkout at `/home/user/fortress`, not a worktree, and a batch's gather stages its files there. While a batch runs, edit nothing tracked there (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order:

0. Check the serving model: run `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh`, which prints the model of this turn's reply. If it prints nothing, use the `get_session` tool with no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If the model is neither Opus nor Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below).
1. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
2. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
3. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
4. The boot note, then the held list.
5. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
6. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.

**A light boot.** When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0 and 3 to 6, and skip steps 1 and 2: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread. Then read the parts of the skills that the work in hand touches, as the boot note names them, if it does. Before you state a fact or a decision, or put anything to the curator, search the record with `facts-extract.sh`. The full boot is the default. The curator's word for a light boot replaces the hook's list of files after a compaction.

- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
  - do no other work until step 0's check shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.

After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could not read the model. Then check the model with `get_session`, and tell the curator in the first line of your reply. If the model is Opus or Fable, go on. If it is not, act as on the alarm.

- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`.
- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.

- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types, and the exclusion test reads its signatures plain. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]`: an open defect (row 695). The rule refuses, rightly, a team declaration, `PureList`'s `List` (row 355); the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator`, which it refused, extends `StandardTotalOrder[\generator\]` since its repair (row 710; `ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss:96`). The compiler's prelude writes the self type instead as `comprises T` on `StandardTotalOrder` and `Equality` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16`, `:24`; on `StandardTotalOrder` since Steele's `655e65d53`, 2012-06-05, and `59fdeff62`, 2012-06-06, which took its F-bound away), and that spelling does not bind the one library, since Naden's last text puts the self-type idiom in bounds only, not as a first-class type (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:626-630`), and Steele's own message on `655e65d53` gives the self type as the trait met with the `comprises` clause, which this rule reads from the F-bound. FACTS.md:125
- F-290 **Outside the twelve, the compiled checker finds 624 component errors in 30 of the library's 40 other components, at least 92 api errors in 10 apis, and 25 crashes.** Measured once on climb batch 22's code, with the distance stage's driver over the components outside the twelve, without the compiler's three files and `GeneratorLibrary`; an api counts only up to its first failing stage. `Avl.fss`, a program kept in the library, stops at name binding on both paths (row 830) and is not among the 40. == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## The goal

POSITIONS.md:12
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over). The step has three parts, and its size is unmeasured. First, walk must run with the Scala checker on; today it runs with it off. Second, walk must evaluate the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, for which it has no case today (F-9 holds both facts). Third, the components that walk's programs import must be cleared of the checker's errors, each before this step or before the first program that needs it (F-290 counts them).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:68
- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.

(** Generic list trait.
    We return a Generator for non-List-specific operations for which
    reuse of the Generator won't increase asymptotic complexity, but
    return a List in cases (such as map and filter) where it will.
*)
trait List[\E\] extends { ZeroIndexed[\E\],
                          LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] } }
        excludes { Number, HasRank, String }
    (** %left% and %extractLeft% return the leftmost element in the list
        (and in the latter case, the remainder of the list without its
---
    complexity, but return a %List% in cases (such as %map% and
    %filter%) where it will.  Indexing on lists operates from the
    left, and ordering is lexicographic reading from the left. *)
trait List[\E\] extends { Equality[\E\], ZeroIndexed[\E\] }
        excludes { Number, HasRank, String }
  (** %left% and %extractLeft% return the leftmost element in the list
      (and in the latter case, the remainder of the list without its
      both lists will be non-empty. *)
  split(): (List[\E\], List[\E\])
  zip[\F\](other: List[\F\]): Generator[\(E,F)\]
  filter(p: E -> Boolean): List[\E\]
  (** %concatMap% is an in-place version of the %nest% method from
---
    complexity, but return a %List% in cases (such as %map% and
    %filter%) where it will.  Indexing on lists operates from the
    left, and ordering is lexicographic reading from the left. *)
trait List[\E\] extends { AnyList, ZeroIndexed[\E\], Equality[\List[\E\]\],

\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
exactly where its elements are totally ordered.
It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{partial-total-orders} says
that a lexicographic order ``may be partial or total depending on whether the
ordering of the elements is partial or total''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex},
lines 520--522), and where the operators chapter's subsection
``Comparisons Operators'' compares lists ``whose elements support these same
comparison operators'', as floating-point numbers do: no partial
lexicographic order of lists is declared.
## In short

- **The question.** The library's `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP` on pairs and triples, and `LexicographicOrder`'s `CMP`, compare elements whose type parameter has no bound. The compiled checker finds no `CMP` on an unbounded parameter: 18 sites (the ways note, section 1), and 8 more clauses it has not read yet behind the `typecase`s.
- **The recommendation.** Two ways, one for each kind, both arms of the fork PLAN item 43 already names.
  - Tuples, now: the ways note's way 1b. Each element type of a pair or triple is bounded by `StandardPartialOrder` (the library's own device for the tuple comparison it typed, `PCMP`, and for the tuple reductions); `Comparison` gains the lazy `LEXICO` that `TotalComparison` already has and the team's compiler prelude declares; each `typecase` gains an `Unordered` clause. 17 sites clear. No checker, walk or specification edit.
  - Lists, at the `where`-clause line: way 3, conditional extension, `List[\E\]` ordered exactly when `E` is, the team's own unbuilt feature, which PLAN's `where`-clause line already names as "item 43's first way". Its one site stays until then.
- **The cost.** One value walk prints changes: `((1,2),3) < ((1,3),0)` answers `true` today and will be refused, because a tuple is outside every trait by the team's own rule, so no bound admits it. Pairs of floats, integers, strings, characters, booleans and lists keep their values. Neither model program compares a tuple or a list.
- **What it reverses or bends.** Nothing on record. It takes item 43's fork by kind, keeps "The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`" whole, and puts the one changed walk value to Pavol before the work, as "Which decisions taken inside the work reach Pavol" asks.
- **The rung.** A library rung of batch 14, one worker, about 20 header lines, 8 clauses, 3 lines of `LEXICO`, one pin replaced, one test added (section 6).

## 2. The ways, weighed

The ways note lists eleven (its section 2). I weigh each against the four positions the brief names, the specification, the later Types chapter and the library's own devices.

**Way 1, bound each element type.** The library's own way for the tuple comparison it typed: Maessen wrote `PCMP` unbounded in 2007 and bounded it per element when he moved it into `RangeInternals` in 2008 (`0948c2b1c`; the ways note, way 1, "The precedent"). The tuple reductions bound each component (`BIG MIN_MIN[\T extends StandardMinMax[\T\], U extends StandardMinMax[\U\]\]`, `.fsi:2011-2027`). The ordered containers bound their element (`Set.fss:25`, `Avl.fss:16`, `QuickSort.fsi:18`, `PrefixMap.fss:37`). At the sites themselves, the type-checker developer's 2008 comment asks for exactly this: "Shouldn't these operators have to extend something? A,B,C?" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4448`

- *1a, total bounds*, loses pairs of floats and rationals (`RR64` and `QQ` are only partial, `.fsi:293`, `:391`): the pin `(1.5, 2) < (2.5, 1)` stops. It also changes the pair `CMP`'s declared type, `Comparison` (`.fsi:2629`), which Maessen fixed to that partial type in 2008 (`98aa8b653`). Not taken.
- *1b, partial bounds*, keeps floats and the declared `Comparison`. Its two extra needs are both in the library's own shape: the lazy `LEXICO` on `Comparison`, which `TotalComparison` and `EqualTo` already declare (`.fss:177`, `:211`) and the team's compiler prelude declares on `Comparison` itself (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:704`, `.fss:1496-1497`, Steele 2011); and an `Unordered` clause in each `typecase`, since under a partial bound the scrutinee's type is `Comparison`, whose `Unordered` case the checker will one day refuse as non-exhaustive ("TODO: A nonexhaustive typecase is an error.", `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:
- *1c, the same bound on `LexicographicOrder`'s element*, forces `List[\E\]` to bound its `E` (`Library/List.fsi:67`), so lists of tuples, functions and `()` could not be written. That contradicts "The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`" ("the library's generic containers are instantiated at tuples") and stops the pins at `ProjectFortress/tests/ResultBoundsRungB.fss:48-59`. Not taken.

**Way 2, lists' order on bounded top-level operators, `Set`'s shape.** It takes `List` out of `StandardTotalOrder`: a `Set`, `Avl` or `quicksort` over lists is refused, lists of lists lose their order, and `List` must regain an `=` of its own or every list assertion falls to identity (`opr =(a:Any, b:Any) = a SEQV b`, `.fss:96`). A restructuring with losses, for one site. Not taken.

**Way 3, conditional extension.** `List[\E\] extends LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`: a list is ordered exactly when its elements are. It is the only way that gives the specification's sentence its meaning, "lexicographic order when used to compare lists whose elements support these same comparison operators" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:294-295`), and the advanced library's "partial or total depending on whether the ordering of the elements is partial or total" (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:520-523`). The grammar has it (`concrete-syntax.tex:465`), the team's test parses it (`ProjectFortress/tests/co

**Way 4, conditional members.** A method's `where` clause on its trait's parameter leaves `LexicographicOrder` extending `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]` unconditionally, so a list of functions would claim an order and lack its operation (the ways note, way 4). For tuples it is way 1. Not taken; way 3 covers it.

**Way 5, tuples ordered structurally by a language rule.** It would make a tuple type a subtype of `StandardTotalOrder[\(A,B)\]`, against "Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types" and "A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than `Any`" (`types-vals-vars.tex:299`, `:306`) and against the designers' later word (`types.tick:341`, `:424`; FACTS, "The team's latest word on types and on the exclusion rule is the unfinished restart"). A type-system change in every area to keep one pinned value. Not taken.

**Way 6, run-time dispatch through an `Any` fallback.** The library's device for `=` (`.fss:96`) and `distribute(r: Any)` (`.fss:3089-3091`). The precedent is weaker than it looks: `=` on `Any` answers a real value, identity, for every value; a `CMP` on `Any` can only throw, and the team's own word for the `distribute` arm is "a hack to avoid the error of overloaded methods". Against "fast code a JVM can specialise", it dispatches per element at run time over arms with F-bounded parameters. Its private form, 6b, needs the compiled dispatcher to choose among two generic arms of different bounds, the shape on which the compiled run dies today (row 537, "Unable to read serialized data", gated f

**Way 7, monomorphic comparisons**, is combinatorial and loses every unwritten combination. **Way 8, an explicit comparator**, has no precedent among the library's operators and loses the operators themselves. **Way 9, drop them**, discards the team's 2007 declarations where its 2008 comment asks for bounds. **Way 10, a checker that defers or re-checks per instance**, revises "If there is no such declaration, then the call is undefined, which is a static error" (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:305-306`) and the checker's modular check, for 18 sites. **Way 11, leave them**, leaves 17 sites that the library's own device clears today. None taken.

The split is by kind because the two kinds differ in what the library can state today. A tuple operator is a top-level function whose own parameters take bounds; the library has written that shape. A list's order is a trait's extends clause, and the condition it needs has no construct yet on either path (FACTS, "The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path ...").
